With ninety students in the first-year architecture studio and only three weeks left in the semester, Professor Lalit Kumar had little time for anyone. But he noticed Chaitanya.
Every other student pinned rough sketches on the review wall; Chaitanya pinned nothing until the final, immaculate board. On Tuesday, when a jury member gave his model 8 out of 10 for a slightly uneven roof, Chaitanya walked out, and Lalit found him crying on the stairs.
That evening Lalit changed his plan. At Wednesday's studio he pinned up his own first sketch for a housing project from years ago: crooked lines, a staircase going nowhere. "This got me a grumpy review," he said. Then he announced a new rule: every student pins a messy sketch by Friday, marked only for effort.
Chaitanya hesitated at the wall for a long time before pinning a pencil drawing with visible erasures. Lalit stopped beside it. "Brave. I like the second window idea."

qa.q: What mark did the jury give Chaitanya's model?
qa.a: 8 out of 10, for a slightly uneven roof.

qa.q: Why might Chaitanya have hesitated so long at the wall on Friday?
qa.a: Pinning a sketch with visible erasures felt risky for someone who only shows immaculate work, so he was likely afraid of being seen as less than perfect.

qa.q: What did Lalit do that helped, despite the big class and little time?
qa.a: He showed his own flawed early sketch, made messy drafts a rule marked for effort, and praised Chaitanya's courage and an idea rather than polish.

qa.q: What might other students have felt seeing their professor's crooked old sketch?
qa.a: They may have felt relieved and amused, and more willing to pin their own rough work without fear.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing a student who never shows drafts and cries over a small mark, and easing the fear by sharing his own mistakes and allowing messy first tries.

passage:
In Naveen Reddy's English class at a college in Himayatnagar, Farhan's essays always arrived on the final day, never a draft before, and they were almost always the best in the room. Last week Farhan got 17 out of 20 and asked to leave the room. Naveen saw him later near the bike stand, eyes red, staring at the paper as though it said 2.
On Monday Naveen brought his own notebook to class, one from his twenties, full of poems with lines struck out and a publisher's rejection slip tucked inside. "I still keep this," he said. "Mistakes are how the good lines got found."
Then he set a new task: a rough, messy draft by Wednesday. "I'll only comment on what you tried, not give a mark."
Farhan's draft came in on Wednesday night, clearly untidy. Naveen wrote back: "Good effort on the argument. Keep going."
The next morning Farhan stayed after class to ask a question.

qa.q: What was tucked inside Naveen's old notebook?
What might Naveen have felt seeing Farhan near the bike stand with red eyes?
qa.a: He was likely concerned to see a strong student crushed by 17 out of 20, which is why he changed his approach on Monday.

qa.q: Which of Naveen's steps might reduce Farhan's fear, and why?
qa.a: Showing his own struck-out poems and rejection slip, and asking for a messy draft with comments only on effort, make mistakes seem normal and safe.

qa.q: How might Farhan have felt receiving 'Good effort on the argument. Keep going.'?
qa.a: He may have felt relieved that an untidy draft brought encouragement instead of judgement, which could be why he stayed to ask a question.

grounding: Illustrates a lecturer who notices a student who never submits drafts and is crushed by a small mark, and responds with his own flawed work and effort-based comments.
